title: Best Low Light Plants for Apartments (and How to Keep Them Alive)
seo_title: Low Light Plants for Apartments: 9 Easy Picks
meta_description: The best low light plants for apartments, with honest care tips, watering guidance, pet safety notes and how to check your light.
body_html:
Not every apartment comes with big, sunny windows. The good news is that several popular houseplants handle dim corners and north-facing rooms well. Here are the best low light plants for apartments, how to care for them and which ones are safe if you have pets.

What "low light" really means

Low light doesn't mean no light. Every plant needs some light to photosynthesize, and none of these will thrive in a windowless bathroom without help.

In practice, low light usually means:

  • A room with a north-facing window.
  • A spot several feet back from a brighter window.
  • A window that's shaded by a building, a tree or a covered balcony.

A quick test: on a sunny day, hold your hand a foot above the spot. If it casts only a faint, fuzzy shadow, you're in low light. If there's barely any shadow at all, consider a grow light (more on that below).

Plants labeled "low light tolerant" survive in these conditions, but most grow more slowly than they would in brighter, indirect light. Slower growth is normal, not a sign you're failing.

9 low light plants that do well in apartments

1. ZZ plant

Glossy leaves and thick rhizomes that store water make the ZZ plant (Zamioculcas zamiifolia) one of the most forgiving houseplants. Let the soil dry out completely between waterings. Overwatering is the main way people kill it. It contains calcium oxalate crystals, so keep it away from pets and kids who might chew it.

2. Snake plant

Snake plants handle low light, dry air and infrequent watering. Water only when the soil is completely dry, which may be every few weeks and even less often in winter. They're toxic to cats and dogs per the ASPCA.

3. Pothos

Pothos trails beautifully from shelves and hanging planters. Water when the top inch or two of soil is dry. In low light, variegated types may lose some of their color, and the vines can get leggy; trim them to encourage fuller growth. Pothos is toxic to cats and dogs per the ASPCA.

4. Cast iron plant

The name says it all. The cast iron plant (Aspidistra elatior) tolerates deep shade, temperature swings and occasional neglect. It grows slowly, so buy one at the size you want. It's listed as non-toxic to cats and dogs by the ASPCA.

5. Parlor palm

A compact palm that does well in lower light and adds a soft, tropical look. Water when the top inch of soil is dry and don't let it sit in soggy soil. The ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to cats and dogs, which makes it a good pick for pet owners.

6. Peace lily

Peace lilies tolerate low light, though they flower more in brighter spots. They droop dramatically when thirsty and perk up soon after watering, which makes them easy to read. Despite the name, they aren't true lilies, but they're still toxic to cats and dogs per the ASPCA.

7. Heartleaf philodendron

Similar to pothos in habit, with softer heart-shaped leaves. Let the top inch or so of soil dry between waterings. Toxic to cats and dogs per the ASPCA.

8. Chinese evergreen

Chinese evergreens (Aglaonema) come in green, silver and pink-tinged varieties. Darker green types generally handle low light better than the brightly colored ones. Keep them away from cold drafts. Toxic to cats and dogs per the ASPCA.

9. Prayer plant

Prayer plants fold their leaves up at night, which is fun to watch. They prefer medium light but tolerate lower light, and they like evenly moist soil and higher humidity. Crispy leaf edges usually mean the air is too dry. The ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to cats and dogs.

Water less in low light

Plants in dim spots use water slowly, so the soil stays wet longer. That's why overwatering, not underwatering, is the most common way low light plants die. Soggy soil leads to root rot.

  • Check before you water. Push a finger into the soil. Don't water on a fixed schedule.
  • Use pots with drainage holes. If you love a decorative pot without one, keep the plant in a plastic nursery pot inside it and dump out any water that collects.
  • Water thoroughly, then let it drain. A deep soak followed by a drying period is better than small sips every few days.
  • Cut back in winter. Growth slows, and so does water use.

Yellowing lower leaves and soil that never seems to dry are classic signs of too much water.

Add a grow light if you need one

If your apartment is truly dark, a full-spectrum LED grow light makes a big difference. Clip-on and bulb-style versions fit standard lamps and look less like lab equipment than they used to.

Put the light on a simple outlet timer so your plants get a consistent day length, and position it fairly close to the plant, following the manufacturer's distance guidance. A smart plug works too; we cover a few in our guide to smart home gadgets for apartments.

Keep pets safe

Many of the easiest low light plants, including pothos, snake plant and peace lily, are toxic to cats and dogs. Chewing on them can cause mouth irritation, drooling and vomiting. If you have pets, either choose non-toxic options like cast iron plant, parlor palm or prayer plant, or keep toxic plants completely out of reach on high shelves or in hanging planters.

Before you buy any new plant, look it up in the ASPCA's toxic and non-toxic plants list. If you think your pet ate part of a toxic plant, call your vet or an animal poison control hotline right away.

Renter tips for plant lovers

  • Protect floors and sills. Put a saucer and a cork or felt pad under every pot. Water that sits on wood floors or windowsills can leave stains your landlord will notice.
  • Hang planters carefully. Ceiling hooks mean holes. Check your lease, or use a tension rod in a window or a freestanding plant stand instead.
  • Group plants together to create a slightly more humid pocket of air, which helps prayer plants and palms.
  • Don't count on plants to purify your air. Plants make a room feel better, but they aren't a substitute for ventilation or an air purifier.

For more ways to make a small space feel calm and lived-in, see our small apartment design ideas and our guide to scents for apartment wellness.

Frequently asked questions

Can plants live in a room with no windows?

Not long-term on their own. With a full-spectrum grow light on a timer, many low light plants, like pothos and ZZ plants, can do well in a windowless room.

What is the easiest low light plant for beginners?

The ZZ plant and snake plant are hard to beat because they tolerate dim light and infrequent watering. Just don't overwater them.

Which low light plants are safe for cats?

Cast iron plant, parlor palm and prayer plant are all listed as non-toxic to cats and dogs by the ASPCA. Always double-check any new plant before you bring it home.

How often should I water plants in low light?

Less often than you think. Check the soil instead of following a schedule, and water only when it has dried to the depth that plant prefers.
